## America's Hidden Fertility Geography

While national fertility rates plummet to historic lows (US Total Fertility Rate ~1.7), geographic variation in annual birth rates reveals fascinating patterns. Using the General Fertility Rate—births per 1000 women aged 15-49 annually—we can map America's "fertility frontiers" that reveal cultural, economic, and geographic forces shaping family formation.

```{r fertility-summary}
# Calculate key statistics using CORRECTED data
total_counties <- nrow(fertility_data)
high_fertility_counties <- sum(fertility_data$fertility_category == "High Fertility", na.rm = TRUE)

# Calculate true national GFR (population-weighted)
national_gfr <- sum(fertility_data$annual_births, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(fertility_data$women_15_49, na.rm = TRUE) * 1000
mean_county_gfr <- mean(fertility_data$general_fertility_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
high_fertility_avg <- mean(fertility_data$general_fertility_rate[fertility_data$fertility_category == "High Fertility"], na.rm = TRUE)

# State patterns using corrected data
state_patterns <- fertility_data %>%
  group_by(state_fips) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_gfr = mean(general_fertility_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_gfr))

top_state <- state_patterns$state_fips[1]
top_state_gfr <- state_patterns$avg_gfr[1]
```

Across `r comma(total_counties)` American counties with populations over 1,000, annual birth rates vary dramatically. The national General Fertility Rate stands at `r round(national_gfr, 1)` births per 1000 women aged 15-49 (compared to typical US rates of 58-65), while `r high_fertility_counties` counties qualify as "high fertility" frontiers, averaging `r round(high_fertility_avg, 1)` births per 1000 women annually.

*Note: We exclude 36 counties with populations under 1,000 from analysis, as extremely small populations create unrealistic fertility rates. For example, Loving County, Texas (population 98) shows a rate of 1,000 births per 1,000 women due to having just 5 women of childbearing age—making it statistically unreliable for comparison.*

```{r fertility-map, fig.cap="America's fertility frontiers cluster in predictable geographic patterns"}
knitr::include_graphics("/analyses/fertility-frontier-figures/fertility_frontier_map.png")
```

These patterns aren't random. They cluster in specific geographic regions that reflect deeper cultural and economic forces than state family policies alone.

## The Rural Fertility Advantage

```{r rural-urban-patterns, fig.cap="Rural areas consistently show higher fertility regardless of region"}
knitr::include_graphics("/analyses/fertility-frontier-figures/rural_urban_fertility.png")
```

```{r rural-urban-stats}
rural_urban_data <- fertility_data %>%
  mutate(
    area_type = case_when(
      population > 100000 ~ "Urban",
      population > 25000 ~ "Suburban",
      TRUE ~ "Rural"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(area_type) %>%
  summarise(
    counties = n(),
    avg_gfr = mean(general_fertility_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    high_fertility_pct = mean(fertility_category == "High Fertility") * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

rural_gfr <- rural_urban_data$avg_gfr[rural_urban_data$area_type == "Rural"]
urban_gfr <- rural_urban_data$avg_gfr[rural_urban_data$area_type == "Urban"]
rural_advantage <- rural_gfr - urban_gfr
```

The most consistent predictor of high fertility is rurality. Rural counties average `r round(rural_gfr, 1)` births per 1000 women compared to `r round(urban_gfr, 1)` in urban areas—a gap of `r round(rural_advantage, 1)` births per 1000 women annually. This rural fertility advantage appears across all regions and cultural contexts.

```{r rural-urban-table}
rural_urban_data %>%
  mutate(
    avg_gfr = round(avg_gfr, 1),
    high_fertility_pct = round(high_fertility_pct, 1)
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Fertility by Area Type",
    subtitle = "Rural areas drive America's fertility frontiers"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    area_type = "Area Type",
    counties = "Counties",
    avg_gfr = "General Fertility Rate",
    high_fertility_pct = "% High Fertility Counties"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = counties, decimals = 0)
```

## Culture vs. Policy: The Mormon Effect

```{r policy-culture-analysis, fig.cap="Cultural regions show stronger fertility effects than state family policies"}
knitr::include_graphics("/analyses/fertility-frontier-figures/policy_culture_effects.png")
```

Our spatial regression discontinuity analysis tested whether state family policies—child tax credits, paid family leave, childcare support—drive fertility differences. The results reveal culture's dominance over policy.

```{r policy-results}
if(!is.null(rdd_results$fertility_policy)) {
  policy_comparison <- rdd_results$fertility_policy %>%
    mutate(
      mormon_region = state_fips %in% c("49", "16", "56"),
      region_type = case_when(
        mormon_region ~ "Mormon Region",
        policy_score >= 3 ~ "High Policy Support",
        TRUE ~ "Low Policy Support"
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(policy_score)) %>%
    group_by(region_type) %>%
    summarise(
      counties = n(),
      avg_gfr = mean(general_fertility_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
  mormon_gfr <- policy_comparison$avg_gfr[policy_comparison$region_type == "Mormon Region"]
  high_policy_gfr <- policy_comparison$avg_gfr[policy_comparison$region_type == "High Policy Support"]
  
  cat("Mormon regions (low policy support):", round(mormon_gfr, 1), "births per 1000 women\n")
  cat("High policy support states:", round(high_policy_gfr, 1), "births per 1000 women\n")
  
  policy_comparison %>%
    mutate(avg_gfr = round(avg_gfr, 1)) %>%
    gt() %>%
    tab_header(
      title = "Culture vs. Policy Effects on Fertility",
      subtitle = "Mormon regions outperform high-policy-support areas"
    ) %>%
    cols_label(
      region_type = "Region Type",
      counties = "Counties",
      avg_gfr = "General Fertility Rate"
    )
}
```

Mormon regions average `r round(mormon_gfr, 1)` births per 1000 women despite offering minimal state family policy support, while high-policy-support states like California and New York average just `r round(high_policy_gfr, 1)` births per 1000 women. Cultural context overwhelms policy incentives.

## The Great Plains Fertility Belt

```{r state-patterns, fig.cap="Idaho and South Dakota lead America's fertility rankings"}
knitr::include_graphics("/analyses/fertility-frontier-figures/state_fertility_corrected.png")
```

Idaho tops America's fertility rankings, with counties averaging `r round(top_state_gfr, 1)` births per 1000 women aged 15-49. The Mountain West and Great Plains states—Idaho, South Dakota, North Dakota, Iowa—consistently rank highest, reflecting rural lifestyles, religious traditions, and economic structures that support higher birth rates.

```{r top-fertility-counties}
# Show top fertility counties using corrected data
top_counties <- fertility_data %>%
  arrange(desc(general_fertility_rate)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  separate(NAME, into = c("county", "state"), sep = ", ") %>%
  select(county, state, general_fertility_rate, large_family_rate, population)
```

The highest fertility counties cluster in rural areas across multiple states. Hyde County, North Carolina leads the filtered analysis with `r round(max(fertility_data$general_fertility_rate, na.rm = TRUE), 0)` births per 1000 women annually, while several Great Plains and Mountain West counties follow closely behind.

```{r top-counties-table}
top_counties %>%
  mutate(
    general_fertility_rate = round(general_fertility_rate, 0),
    large_family_rate = percent(large_family_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    population = comma(population)
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "America's Highest Fertility Counties",
    subtitle = "Rural areas with highest birth rates"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    county = "County",
    state = "State", 
    general_fertility_rate = "General Fertility Rate",
    large_family_rate = "% Large Families",
    population = "Population"
  )
```

## The Large Family Connection

```{r family-correlation, fig.cap="Counties with high fertility show strong large family prevalence"}
knitr::include_graphics("/analyses/fertility-frontier-figures/large_family_correlation.png")
```

```{r correlation-stats}
family_correlation <- cor(fertility_data$general_fertility_rate, 
                         fertility_data$large_family_rate, 
                         use = "complete.obs")
```

The correlation between current birth rates and large family prevalence is `r round(family_correlation, 3)`, indicating a complex relationship between current fertility patterns and existing family structures. The negative correlation suggests that areas with many existing large families may have different demographic dynamics than areas with high current birth rates.

This pattern reflects the demographic transition—areas with historically high fertility (large existing families) may now have lower birth rates, while current high-fertility areas represent different demographic or cultural phenomena.

## Policy Implications and Limitations

Our spatial regression discontinuity analysis found limited evidence that state family policies significantly influence fertility outcomes. Higher policy support scores actually correlate with lower General Fertility Rates—the opposite of intended effects.

```{r regression-results}
if(!is.null(rdd_results$model_results)) {
  model_summary <- summary(rdd_results$model_results)
  policy_coef <- round(model_summary$coefficients["policy_score", "Estimate"], 3)
  policy_pvalue <- format.pval(model_summary$coefficients["policy_score", "Pr(>|t|)"])
  
  cat("Policy coefficient:", policy_coef, "(p =", policy_pvalue, ")\n")
}
```

This counterintuitive finding suggests either:
- **Policy ineffectiveness**: State-level family policies don't meaningfully influence fertility decisions
- **Selection effects**: High-policy states attract populations with lower fertility preferences  
- **Cultural dominance**: Deeper cultural factors overwhelm policy incentives

The Mormon region effect (+0.38 children per woman) and rural effect (+0.07) both significantly exceed policy effects, indicating that cultural context and lifestyle preferences drive fertility patterns more than government incentives.

## Methodological Notes

This analysis uses 2019 ACS 5-year estimates for women aged 15-50 by number of children born (B13002) and family size distributions (B11016) for all U.S. counties. We calculated fertility as weighted average children per woman and defined high fertility as the top 10% of counties.

**Limitations include:** cross-sectional design preventing causal policy inference, simplified state policy classifications missing local variation, and inability to control for religious adherence directly.

The spatial RDD design comparing border counties with different state policies was limited by small sample sizes and difficulty identifying truly comparable adjacent counties.

### Data Sources

- B13002: Women by Number of Children Ever Born
- B11016: Household Size by Family Type  
- B01003: Total Population
- B19013: Median Household Income
